Its unyielding strength stands for the hero's unchallenged identity.

name: Crown of Ariadne
powers: Set among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis after Ariadne's death.
description: The golden crown Ariadne wore when Theseus rescued her from Crete; Dionysus later set it in the heavens as the constellation Corona Borealis. Catullus and later poets tell how the crown commemorates the abandoned bride of Naxos, transformed into a circlet of stars.

name: Shield of Aeneas
powers: Shows the future of Rome, from Romulus to the triumph of Augustus at Actium.
description: The shield Vulcan forged for Aeneas, engraved with the future of Rome: Romulus and Remus, the rape of the Sabines, and the triumph of Augustus at Actium. Virgil describes it at the close of Aeneid 8 as the destiny of the Trojan line made visible in bronze.

name: Sibylline Books
powers: Prophetic verses consulted by the Roman state to avert calamities; their burning punished Tarquin's haggling.
description: The nine books of prophetic verses the Cumaean Sibyl offered to Tarquinius Superbus, of which she burned six and sold the last three at the original price, as Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus relate; kept in the temple of Jupiter, the surviving Sibylline Books were consulted for Rome's most dangerous crises.
source: Livy, History of Rome; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities

name: Lituus of Romulus
powers: Marked the regions of the sky for augury at Rome's foundation; found unharmed after the burning of the Curia Saliorum.
description: The curved augur's staff with which Romulus marked out the regions of the sky when founding Rome; kept in the Curia Saliorum on the Palatine, it was found unharmed after the temple burned, a portent of Rome's safety. Cicero and Plutarch record the relic, and augurs carried the lituus as the mark of their office.
source: Cicero, De Divinatione; Plutarch, Life of Camillus; Dionysius of Halicarnassus

name: Ancile
maker: Fell from heaven in the reign of Numa; copies made by the smith Mamurius Veturius
powers: Pledge of Rome's eternity; twelve copies kept the true shield hidden from thieves.
description: The sacred shield of Mars that fell from heaven in the reign of Numa, taken as a pledge of Rome's eternity; Numa had eleven identical copies made so that thieves could not identify it, and the Salii guarded and carried all twelve in the March procession. Plutarch, Ovid, and Servius tell the legend.
source: Plutarch, Life of Numa; Ovid, Fasti (Book 3); Servius, on the Aeneid

name: Golden Bough
maker: Hidden in the wood of Proserpina
powers: Admitted a living man into the underworld; the offering Proserpina required of Aeneas.
description: The golden bough Aeneas plucked in the Sibyl's wood to gain entry to the underworld and offer to Proserpina; like mistletoe it must be found and plucked by fate alone, and its presence admits the living to the realm of the dead. Virgil makes it the passport of the Aeneid's descent.

name: Arrows of Cupid
powers: The golden arrow kindles love; the blunt leaden one drives love away.
description: The arrows of Cupid in Ovid's Metamorphoses: the golden-headed shaft that kindles love and the blunt leaden one that drives love away. Apollo, struck by the golden, chases Daphne, who flees because of the leaden; the two arrows explain uncontrollable passion in Roman myth.

name: Sword of Damocles
maker: Hung at the court of Dionysius II of Syracuse
powers: Showed Damocles the peril hidden in royal ease; the emblem of insecurity in power.
description: The sword suspended by a single horse-hair over the head of Damocles, courtier of Dionysius II of Syracuse, to show him the insecurity of royal power; when Damocles envied the tyrant's life, Dionysius made him taste it, and the hanging sword became the emblem of peril in high office. Told by Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations.

name: Corona Civica
material: Oak leaves (holm, esculent, or common oak)
powers: Rewarded a soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground; granted lifelong honour and the right to sit with senators.
description: The Roman civic crown of oak leaves, second only to the grass crown in honour, awarded to a soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle and held the ground; the inscription 'ob cives servatos' and the right to wear it for life made it Rome's most coveted decoration, described by Pliny and Aulus Gellius.
source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History (Book 16); Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights (Book 5)

name: Liver of Piacenza
powers: Model of a sheep's liver used in hepatoscopy; its sixteen inscribed zones map the heavens onto the organ.
description: The life-sized bronze model of a sheep's liver, found near Piacenza in 1877 and dated to the late 2nd-early 1st century BC, its surface divided into sixteen inscribed zones naming Etruscan gods; used by haruspices to teach and perform hepatoscopy, reading the future from the liver's form. It is the key artifact of Etruscan divination.
source: Archaeological find (Gossolengo, 1877; Museo Civico di Palazzo Farnese, Piacenza)

name: Pyrgi Gold Plaques
maker: Dedicated by Thefarie Velianas of Caere
powers: Bilingual dedicatory texts linking the Etruscan goddess Uni with the Phoenician Astarte; cornerstone of Etruscan language study.
description: Three gold sheets found in 1964 at the Etruscan port of Pyrgi, inscribed about 500 BC in Etruscan and Phoenician, recording Thefarie Velianas' dedication of Temple B to Uni, identified with Astarte; the bilingual text is one of the oldest historical documents from Italy and a cornerstone for understanding the Etruscan language.
source: Archaeological find (Pyrgi, Santa Severa, 1964; Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome)

name: Tizona
material: Iron and steel blade with silver-gilt hilt
maker: Blade of Andalusian manufacture, c. 11th century
powers: Sword of El Cid won from King Yucef of Valencia; 'worth a thousand marks of gold' in the Cantar.
description: The sword Tizona, named in the Cantar de Mio Cid as El Cid's blade won from King Yucef of Valencia; the sword shown in the Museo de Burgos has an 11th-century blade, though its hilt and inscriptions are later additions, so its link to Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar rests on legend rather than proof.
source: Cantar de Mio Cid; Museo de Burgos (provenance and metallurgical studies)

name: Chest of El Cid
powers: A ruse: sand offered as treasure to raise funds from the moneylenders Rachel and Vidas.
description: The chest of El Cid in the Cantar de Mio Cid, filled with sand, pawned to the moneylenders Rachel and Vidas as a supposed hoard of treasure to raise funds for exile; the ruse displays the hero's cunning and was never meant to be redeemed, a famous comic episode of the Spanish epic.

name: Santo Caliz
material: Agate cup with gold mounts, pearls, and gems
era: Agate cup of the 2nd-1st century BC; mounts medieval
maker: Unknown Hellenistic or Roman lapidary; goldwork by later craftsmen
powers: Venerated as the cup of the Last Supper; its identification is tradition, not verified history.
description: The Holy Chalice of Valencia, an agate cup of the 2nd-1st century BC set in medieval gold mounts, kept in Valencia Cathedral since 1437; tradition identifies it as the cup of the Last Supper, brought from Jerusalem via Rome and Huesca, but that identification cannot be verified and is disputed. The cup itself is genuine and ancient.
source: Valencia Cathedral tradition; A. Beltran, archaeological study (1960)

name: Rooster of Barcelos
material: Legendary roast fowl; modern ceramic replicas
powers: A roasted rooster rose and crowed to prove a condemned pilgrim's innocence.
description: The Rooster of Barcelos, from the Portuguese legend of a Galician pilgrim wrongly condemned to hang in Barcelos; before the judge, the pilgrim swore his innocence by the roasted rooster on the table, and the bird rose and crowed. The miracle saved him, and the ceramic Galo de Barcelos became a national symbol.
source: Portuguese oral tradition; collected versions of the Barcelos legend

name: Nau Catrineta
era: Folk era (legend set in the Age of Sail)
powers: Lost at sea until an angel saved the captain and the ship reached port.
description: The legendary ship of the Portuguese romance 'Nau Catrineta', lost at sea for seven years until the crew drew lots to sacrifice the captain-general; the devil, disguised as the lookout, demanded his soul, but an angel saved him and the ship reached port. Recorded in Almeida Garrett's Romanceiro, the ballad survives in many oral versions.
source: Portuguese oral tradition; Almeida Garrett, Romanceiro

name: Portuguese Guitar
material: Wood, metal strings (twelve strings in six courses)
maker: Developed from the English cittern in Lisbon
powers: The signature voice of fado, said to express saudade itself.
description: The Portuguese guitar, a twelve-string cittern with a pear-shaped body, the defining instrument of fado; its bright, plaintive sound accompanies the singer in Lisbon's taverns and is said to voice saudade itself. A documented tradition of urban song rather than a mythic relic, it anchors Portugal's musical folklore.
source: Ethnographic and musicological documentation of the fado tradition

name: Nazar Boncugu
powers: Deflects the envious gaze of the nazar (evil eye).
description: The nazar boncugu, the blue-and-white glass evil-eye bead of Turkey, worn as jewellery or hung in homes and on vehicles to deflect the envious gaze of the nazar; its counter-charm is a documented folk practice tied to the Mediterranean belief in the evil eye, and it remains the most widespread Turkish protective amulet.

name: Karagoz
material: Dyed translucent leather (camel hide) on a stick
powers: Comic everyman of the shadow screen, bickering with Hacivat in plays performed behind a lit panel.
description: Karagoz, the shadow puppet of Ottoman Turkish theatre, a comic everyman who bickers with his friend Hacivat in the traditional play; the translucent leather puppets are worked behind a lit screen and the whole form takes its name from the main character, said to have been an ironworker whose antics amused the Sultan. A living oral-dramatic tradition of Turkey.
source: Turkish oral tradition and documented Ottoman shadow theatre

name: Talismanic Shirt
material: Cotton or linen, painted with ink and gold
powers: Worn next to the skin to shield the wearer from wounds, illness, and evil in battle.
description: The tilsimli gomlek, or talismanic shirt, a cotton garment painted with Qur'anic verses, magic squares, and astrological signs, worn next to the skin by Ottoman sultans for protection in battle; some eighty survive in the Topkapi collection, including Cem Sultan's shirt begun in 1477, whose astrological moment of making is inscribed in it.
source: Topkapi Palace Museum collection; Tezcan, Tilsimli Gomlekler

name: Mehter Davul
material: Wooden shell with skin heads, struck with a beater
powers: Beats the rhythm of the janissary march, inspiring troops and intimidating the enemy.
description: The great bass drum of the mehter, the Ottoman military band, slung and struck to beat the rhythm of the janissary march; its booming sound, with the zurna, was meant to inspire troops and terrify the enemy in battle, and the mehter davul remains an emblem of Ottoman martial music.
source: Ottoman musical tradition; documentation of the mehter band

name: Gusle
material: Maple bowl, single horse-hair string, horse-hair bow
powers: Accompanied heroic epic song in the oral tradition of the southern Balkans.
description: The gusle, a single-stringed fiddle of the Balkan epic singers, played with a bow while the singer chants heroic songs; on the Croatian coast and hinterland it accompanied tales of heroes and outlaws, and the instrument is inseparable from the region's oral heroic tradition, documented among Croats, Serbs, and Montenegrins.
source: Ethnographic documentation of the South Slavic epic tradition

name: Croatian Nosnja
material: Linen, wool, and embroidery, varying by region
powers: Carried the wearer's village, age, and marital status in its cut, colour, and embroidery.
description: The Croatian nosnja, the traditional folk costume of the country's regions, worn for feast days and festivals; each district had its own cut, embroidery, and colours, and the costume carried the wearer's place, age, and status. Documented ethnographically, it is a garment of identity in Croatian folklore rather than a single mythic object.
source: Ethnographic documentation of Croatian regional costume

name: Luzzu
era: Traditional working boat (modern form early 20th century)
maker: Maltese boatwrights, family yards at Marsaxlokk and Gozo
powers: The painted Eye of Osiris on the prow wards off the evil eye and guides the boat home.
description: The luzzu, the brightly painted wooden fishing boat of the Maltese islands, whose prow carries a pair of apotropaic eyes known as the Eye of Osiris or of Horus, an inheritance from Phoenician seafaring meant to ward off the evil eye and guide the boat home; the working fleets of Marsaxlokk still sail with the painted gaze.
source: Ethnographic and maritime documentation of the Maltese fishing tradition

name: Ivory Statue of Galatea
powers: Brought to life by Aphrodite at Pygmalion's prayer; became his wife.
description: The ivory statue the sculptor Pygmalion of Cyprus carved and fell in love with; at his prayer Aphrodite brought it to life as Galatea, who became his wife. Ovid's Metamorphoses tells the story, the classic tale of art animated by desire, and it is set on the island of Cyprus.

name: Caladbolg
powers: Legendary sword of Cú Chulainn, capable of slicing the head off a boar with a single stroke.
description: The famed sword Caladbolg, wielded by the hero Cú Chulainn in the Ulster Cycle, renowned for its sharpness and lethal edge. It appears in the tale of Ferdiad where Cú Chulainn uses it to cut the head off his opponent.

name: Hermes’ Sandals
powers: Grants the wearer winged speed and the ability to travel instantly across realms.
description: The winged sandals of Hermes, the messenger god, enable swift travel and serve as a symbol of speed and cunning in Greek mythology.

name: Aegis
powers: Provides impenetrable protection and bears the terrifying visage of Medusa.
description: The Aegis is Zeus's shield, forged by Hephaestus, famed for its protective power and fearsome appearance.

name: Caduceus
powers: Symbolizes negotiation and safe passage; restores harmony.
description: The Caduceus is the winged staff carried by Hermes, representing trade, negotiation, and safe journeys.

name: Ankh
powers: Symbol of life; grants vitality to the bearer.
description: The ankh is a looped cross symbol widely used in ancient Egyptian art, representing the concept of eternal life. It appears in tomb paintings and temple reliefs held by deities and pharaohs alike, signifying their divine right to live forever.

name: Scarab Amulet
powers: Protection against evil; associated with rebirth.
description: A scarab-shaped amulet crafted from glazed faience, representing the beetle god Khepri who rolls the sun across the sky. Such amulets were placed in burials to ensure safe passage and rebirth in the afterlife.

name: Scepter of Ra
powers: Authority of the sun god; used in prayers and royal ceremonies.
description: The Was scepter, a long staff with a forked tip, was the emblem of power and dominion of the sun god Ra. It appears in temple reliefs and on royal crowns, symbolizing the pharaoh's role as the earthly representative of Ra.

name: Jade Dragon
powers: Symbol of imperial authority and protection; believed to ward off evil spirits.
description: A finely carved jade dragon pendant used by nobles during the Han Dynasty. The dragon motif represented celestial power and was worn as a talisman to ensure the bearer's prestige and safety.

name: Yumi Bow
powers: Exceptional range and accuracy; used in court archery contests.
description: The yumi is a tall asymmetrical bow used by samurai and nobles. Its distinctive shape allowed for powerful shots and was a status symbol in Heian-era archery tournaments.

name: Heian Court Fan
powers: Elegant signaling device; used in court dances and ceremonies.
description: A delicate folding fan employed by Heian courtiers to convey subtle messages and as an accessory in classical dances. Its painted motifs often depict seasonal scenes.

name: Excalibur
powers: Blade that cut through any armor; scabbard protected the wearer from wounding.
description: The great sword of King Arthur, given to him by the Lady of the Lake and returned to her waters after his death at Camlann. In Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur its scabbard protects the wearer from wounding. The name also attaches to the sword Arthur drew from the stone in later romance.

name: Claíomh Mór
powers: Said to bite through any armor or shield.
description: Claíomh Mór, the 'great sword' of Irish tradition, one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried into Ireland and linked with Nuada Airgetlám. Later lore gives it a blade that could pierce any armour or shield. The name is close to, and often confused with, Claíomh Solais, the sword of light.

name: Dyrnwyn
powers: Burst into flame when drawn by a worthy man; burned the unworthy bearer.
description: Dyrnwyn, the sword of Rhydderch Hael, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Drawn by a worthy man it burst into flame; drawn by an unworthy bearer it burned the wielder himself. A noble warrior is said to have taken it, though later tradition preserves few details of its fate.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Gáe Assail
powers: Unstoppable spear of the champion of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
description: Gáe Assail, the great spear of Lugh, one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried into Ireland. Lugh used it at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, where it helped rout the Fomorians. Its name preserves an older association with the Otherworld gift-bearers of Irish tradition.

name: The Green Knight's Axe
powers: Weapon of the beheading challenge at Camelot.
description: The enormous green-steel axe carried by the Green Knight into King Arthur's hall at the start of the fourteenth-century poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Gawain strikes the Knight's head off with it, and the Knight picks up the severed head, which reminds Gawain of the return blow owed at the Green Chapel.
source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (fourteenth century)

name: Durendal
powers: Indestructible blade whose pommel holds relics of Saint Peter, Saint Basil and Saint Denis.
description: Durendal, Roland's sword in the eleventh-century Chanson de Roland. Its gilded pommel holds a tooth of Saint Peter, blood of Saint Basil and hair of Saint Denis. Wounded at Roncevaux, Roland tries to break it against a rock rather than let it fall to the Saracens; the blade survives and the rock splits.

name: Szczerbiec
powers: Symbol of Polish kingship; the notched blade carries the Kiev legend.
description: Szczerbiec, the jagged sword used at Polish coronations from the Middle Ages. Its name, 'the notched one', recalls the legend that Bolesław the Brave struck it against the Golden Gate of Kiev in 1018. The surviving blade, now in Wawel Castle, was damaged in a nineteenth-century theft.

name: Sword of Attila
material: Iron with gold and gem-set hilt
powers: Blade of world dominion pledged to Attila.
description: The sword said to have belonged to Attila the Hun and kept among Hungarian royal treasures. The Roman historian Jordanes records that a shepherd found a blade in the ground that Attila called the Sword of Mars, pledge of world dominion. The gilded iron saber shown in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum is identified with it in later tradition.

name: Tara Brooch
material: Silver-gilt, gold filigree, amber and glass
description: The Tara Brooch, a richly filigreed silver-and-gold annular brooch made around the eighth century. It was discovered in 1850 on the beach at Bettystown, County Meath, and the name 'Tara' was attached for sale because of the site's royal associations. It survives in the National Museum of Ireland with its original chain intact.

name: Great Torc of Snettisham
description: The Great Torc of Snettisham, a necklace of two interlocking gold-alloy rings with ornate buffer terminals, made in eastern England around 75 BC and found in a hoard at Snettisham, Norfolk, in 1950. Such tores marked high status among Iron Age Britons; the example is a centrepiece of the British Museum's Celtic collection.

name: Claddagh Ring
description: The Claddagh, a ring shaped as two hands holding a heart beneath a crown, made in Galway since at least the seventeenth century. The popular story of Richard Joyce, enslaved in Algiers, who sent one home, is late and unverifiable; older written records of the motif are scarce, so the origin legend is treated as tradition rather than fact.

name: Crown of Saint Wenceslas
material: Gold set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds
description: The Crown of Saint Wenceslas, made in 1347 for Charles IV and used to crown Bohemian kings. It is set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds and kept with the other Czech crown jewels. Legend holds that any usurper who sets it on his head will die within a year; it is shown only rarely and under strict conditions.

name: Ship of the Flying Dutchman
powers: Doomed to sail the Cape of Good Hope forever; sighting it is an omen.
description: The ghost ship of the Flying Dutchman, a spectral East Indiaman doomed to round the Cape of Good Hope forever after its captain, variously named Van der Decken, swore against the wind in a storm. Sightings were reported from the seventeenth century onward; no physical vessel exists, and the tale is maritime legend.
source: Maritime legend, from the seventeenth century

name: Prydwen
powers: Arthur's vessel for voyages to the Otherworld stronghold of Annwn.
description: Prydwen, the ship of King Arthur in Welsh tradition. In Culhwch ac Olwen Arthur sails in Prydwen, and the poem Preiddeu Annwn describes Arthur's fleet journey to the Otherworld fortress of Annwn. Welsh sources also give the name to a shield, showing the word shifted between ship and protection.

name: Mantle of Tegau Eurfron
powers: Fitted only a wife faithful to her husband; exposed unfaithful wives.
description: Tegau Eurfron's mantle, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. It would fall only to a wife faithful to her husband; for a woman who had broken her vows it would not cover her, and the truth of her conduct was laid bare. It is the Welsh counterpart of the chastity-testing garments of continental romance.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Arthur's Mantle
powers: Made the wearer invisible while still allowing them to see everything around them.
description: Arthur's mantle, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whoever wore it became invisible, though the wearer could still see everything about them. The mantle belongs to the Arthur of the medieval Welsh marvel-list tradition, distinct from the later continental Arthur of Malory, and is recorded only in the Welsh treasure catalogue.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Tarnhelm
powers: Rendered the wearer invisible.
description: Tarnhelm, the magic cap of invisibility in the Nibelungenlied. Siegfried takes it from the dwarf Alberich along with the Nibelung hoard; it lets him work unseen. Richard Wagner later gave the name to the golden ring's forging helmet in the Ring cycle, where it also allows shape-shifting, a power absent from the medieval poem.

name: Selkie's Seal-Skin
powers: Lets the selkie shed human form and return to the sea when put back on.
description: The seal-skin of the selkie, the shapeshifting seal-people of Scottish and Irish tradition. A selkie sheds the skin to take human form on land and must have it returned to go back to the sea; a human who hides the skin keeps the selkie as a spouse until the skin is found. The motif underpins the classic selkie-bride tales.

name: Silver Branch of Emain
powers: Its music lulled listeners and summoned heroes to the Otherworld.
description: The silver apple-branch carried by a woman of the Otherworld to the hero Bran in the medieval tale the Voyage of Bran. Its music lulls those who hear it, and Bran leaves with its bearer for the Land of Women across the sea. Messengers of the Irish Otherworld traditionally bear such singing branches.

name: Cormac's Cup
powers: Shattered at a spoken lie and restored itself when truth was told.
description: The cup given to the high king Cormac mac Airt in Echtra Cormaic, offered by a warrior who proves to be Manannán mac Lir. It shatters when a lie is spoken and restores itself when the truth is told, allowing Cormac to test the words of his court. It is one of the moral test-objects of Irish wonder literature.
source: Echtra Cormaic (The Adventure of Cormac mac Airt)

name: Frau Holle's Feather Bed
powers: Shaken by Frau Holle, its feathers fall to earth as snow.
description: Frau Holle's feather bed, the great bedding the old woman shakes in the Grimm tale of the same name. Each time she shakes it the feathers fall as snow, which is why, the tale explains, snow falls in winter. The heroine earns it through service; the episode is the story's comic explanation of the seasons.

name: Franks Casket
description: The Franks Casket, an eighth-century Anglo-Saxon chest carved from whalebone, covered with scenes from Germanic legend, the Bible and classical history, with runic and Latin inscriptions. The front panel shows the smith Weland being released by a maiden he rescued. It was bought in the nineteenth century and is now in the British Museum.

name: Cauldron of Rebirth
powers: Restored slain warriors to life, though the revived could not speak.
description: Pair Dadeni, the Cauldron of Rebirth in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi. Given to Brân the Blessed by a giant couple from Ireland, it restores slain warriors to life, though the revived cannot speak. In the war for Branwen the cauldron is finally shattered by Efnysien, who throws himself into it.

name: Cauldron of the Dagda
powers: No company ever went away from it unsatisfied.
description: Coire an Dagda, the Dagda's cauldron, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann. It is the cauldron of plenty: no company ever went away from it unsatisfied. With the spear of Lugh, the stone of Fal and the sword of Nuada it ranks among the wonder-gifts carried into Ireland by the Old Gods.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann

name: Lia Fáil
powers: Cried out beneath the rightful king of Ireland when he stood on it.
description: Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny at the hill of Tara, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann. In tradition it cried out beneath the rightful king of Ireland when he stood on it. The medieval account of the coronation of Conn is the best-known instance of the stone's voice.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Baile in Scáil

name: Ardagh Chalice
material: Silver, bronze, gold filigree, glass and enamel
description: The Ardagh Chalice, a silver-and-bronze liturgical cup made around the eighth century, found in 1868 in a ring-fort at Ardagh, County Limerick, with a hoard of other church metalwork. Its decorated panels of gold filigree, glass and enamel mark it as a masterpiece of Insular art; it is held by the National Museum of Ireland.

name: The Grail of Peredur
description: The dish or salver carried in the procession at the castle of Peredur in the medieval Welsh romance that bears his name. Unlike the French Grail romances, the Welsh text describes a bleeding head on a salver and a woman carrying a dish, a version that preserves a distinct Celtic Arthurian strand. The item is legendary and unattested.

name: Nanteos Cup
description: The Nanteos Cup, a late medieval wooden mazer bowl kept for two centuries at Nanteos mansion in Ceredigion and treated as a healing cup. Sick pilgrims were said to drink from it, and its gradual erosion was blamed on those who bit or scraped it. Claims that it was the Holy Grail began only in the nineteenth century and remain unverified.

name: Ceridwen's Cauldron
powers: Brewed the Awen, the drops of inspiration and knowledge, for a year and a day.
description: Ceridwen's cauldron in the medieval Tale of Taliesin, in which the goddess-figure Ceridwen brews a potion of inspiration for her son for a year and a day. The three drops fall on Gwion, who swallows them and gains the Awen before being transformed and pursued through animal shapes. The cauldron is wholly legendary.

name: Pied Piper's Pipe
powers: Its music charmed rats, and later children, following the piper out of Hamelin.
description: The pipe of the Pied Piper of Hamelin, the instrument whose music lured the town's rats to the river Weser, and then, when the townsfolk refused payment, drew the children away into a mountainside. No actual pipe survives; it belongs to the semi-legendary 1284 Hamelin tradition and its later retellings.
source: Hamelin tradition; Grimm and Browning retellings

name: Green Knight's Holly Branch
description: The holly branch carried by the Green Knight in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight when he rides unarmed into Arthur's hall. Its evergreen branches mark him as one of the winter gods of the older year, and he uses it to hold his own axe as he delivers his challenge. It is an emblem of the poem's beheading-game and seasonal cycle.
source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

name: The Round Table
powers: Seated all the knights of Arthur's court without quarrels over precedence.
description: The Round Table of King Arthur, the great table at which none of the knights could claim a higher seat than another. In Geoffrey of Monmouth it is a table of guests; in later romance the table, like Arthur's court, is divided when Merlin reads the fate of a knight who will win the Grail. A 13th-century table at Winchester is linked to the legend.
source: Geoffrey of Monmouth; Arthurian romance; Winchester table

name: The Singing Harp
powers: Sang on its own and cried out for its master, waking the giant.
description: The singing golden harp of the giant in the tale of Jack and the Beanstalk. As Jack climbs down the beanstalk with the hen and the gold, the harp calls out for its master, waking the giant and setting the chase in motion. It is one of the three treasures the giant keeps in his castle.
source: Jack and the Beanstalk (English fairy tale)

name: The Magic Mirror
powers: Told its owner who was the fairest in the land.
description: The magic mirror of the queen in the Grimm tale of Snow White. Each time she asks 'Mirror, mirror on the wall, who is the fairest of them all?', the mirror answers truly, and its answer drives the queen to send Snow White into the wood. The mirror is a test-object of the tale and exists only in fiction.

name: Cinderella's Glass Slipper
powers: Fitted only Cinderella, letting the prince find her after the ball.
description: The glass slipper in the Grimms' Aschenputtel, the shoe lost as Cinderella flees the prince's ball. Because it fits no other foot in the kingdom, it lets the prince find his bride. Perrault's version makes the slipper glass; the object is a fairy-tale token and no such slipper survives.
source: Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen no. 21; Perrault

name: The Six Swans' Shirts
powers: Thrown over her swan brothers, restored them to human form.
description: The six shirts of stinging nettles woven in silence by the sister in the Grimms' tale of the six swans. For years she must sew them without speaking a word; when at last they are thrown over her brothers, the swans become men again. The shirt-making is the tale's central task and ordeal.

name: Briar Rose's Spinning Wheel
powers: Pricked the princess and cast the whole castle into a hundred-year sleep.
description: The spinning wheel in the Grimms' Dornröschen, whose spindle pricks the sleeping princess and sends the entire castle into a century of sleep. The king had ordered all spindles burned, but the old woman in the tower still spins. When the prince cuts through the thorns, the spindle's pricking is undone and the wheel stands still.

name: The Golden Goose
powers: Stuck fast anyone who touched it, drawing a growing chain of followers.
description: Die goldene Gans, the goose from the Grimms' tale of the same name. Found by Dummling in the wood, the golden goose sticks fast to anyone who touches it, so that the whole town follows in a chain behind him; the sight makes the sad princess laugh, winning her hand. The goose is a purely fictional marvel.

name: The Papyrus of Ani
aliases: Book of the Dead of Ani
maker: Scribes of Thebes for the scribe Ani
powers: Guides the deceased through the judgment of the afterlife.
description: The finest surviving Book of the Dead manuscript, commissioned for the Theban scribe Ani around 1250 BCE. Its long roll of vignettes and hieroglyphic spells was meant to guide the dead through the afterlife, most famously the weighing of the heart against the feather of Ma'at in chapter 125, with Ani and his wife shown before the gods. It is the classic witness to Egyptian funerary literature.
source: The Book of the Dead (Papyrus of Ani), British Museum EA 10470

name: Eye of Horus
powers: Protects the wearer and restores wholeness; the healed eye of the falcon god.
description: The wedjat, the eye that the god Thoth healed after Set tore it from Horus, worn as an amulet of protection, healing, and wholeness. Its hieroglyphic fractions were used for measuring grain volumes, and thousands of wedjat amulets in faience, gold, and stone survive in tombs from the Old Kingdom into the Graeco-Roman period, where the sign still guarded the living and the dead.
source: Egyptian amulets and temple reliefs; Pyramid Texts

name: The Scales of Ma'at
powers: Weighs the heart of the dead against the feather of truth in the judgment hall.
description: The great balance set up in the Hall of Two Truths, where the heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of Ma'at before Osiris, with Thoth recording the result. Chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead describes the rite, while the devourer Ammit waits to swallow any heart found heavier than the feather. The scene is among the most reproduced images of Egyptian religion.

name: The Feather of Ma'at
powers: The counterweight of truth against which the heart of the dead is weighed.
description: The ostrich feather worn on the head of the goddess Ma'at, placed on the scales of judgment as the counterweight to the heart of the dead. A heart lighter than the feather passed on to the afterlife; a heavier one was devoured by Ammit. The feather, also worn by the god Shu in his role of lifting the sky, became the emblem of a life measured by truth.

name: The Golden Falcon of Hierakonpolis
powers: The earliest great image of the falcon god Horus.
description: A gold head of the falcon god Horus found in the main deposit of the temple at Hierakonpolis, dated to about 3100 BCE, one of the oldest large cult images of a deity to survive from Egypt. With its obsidian eyes and worked gold feathers, it stood as the focus of worship at the site where the Narmer Palette was also found, marking the beginnings of pharaonic divine kingship.

name: The Sistrum
powers: Its rattling pleased the goddess and drove away hostile powers.
description: A sacred rattle of looped bronze rods strung across a frame, shaken in the cult of Hathor and Isis to please the goddess and repel evil with its hissing sound. Priestesses, queens, and kings bore it in temple ritual, and great ceremonial versions stood as temple furniture. Its naos-shaped variant carried the cow-eared head of Hathor between its handles and remained in use into Graeco-Roman Egypt.

name: The Crook and Flail
aliases: Shepherd's Crook and Flail of Osiris
material: Gold and blue faience (mythic and royal)
powers: Signs of kingship and of Osiris's shepherd-care over the people.
description: The crossed crook (heka) and flail (nekhakha) carried by Osiris as emblems of royal authority and of the shepherd's care for his flock, laid crossed over royal mummies. Temple reliefs show the living pharaoh handing the pair to the god of the dead and receiving it back, and gilt examples were buried with kings such as Tutankhamun. Together they fix the image of the enthroned Osiris.

name: The Solar Barque of Ra
powers: Carries the sun across the sky by day and through the underworld by night.
description: The two celestial boats in which the sun god Ra sails: the day barque Mandjet crossing the sky and the night barque Mesektet crossing the Duat, where the crew repels the serpent Apep with spears. The nightly battle myth inspired real solar barques buried beside temples and pyramids, including the Khufu boat, so that the king might make the same journey after death.
source: Pyramid Texts and solar barque burials

name: Ushabti Figurines
powers: Answer the summons to labor in the afterlife in place of the deceased.
description: Small mummiform figurines placed in Egyptian tombs to perform field labor for the dead in the afterlife, inscribed with spell 6 of the Book of the Dead, in which the figure answers 'here I am' when summoned to work. A single burial could hold several hundred, from a modest clay set to the 413 ushabtis of Tutankhamun. The name derives from the Egyptian word for 'answerer.'
source: Book of the Dead, spell 6; tomb assemblages

name: The Djed Pillar
powers: Symbol of stability and of the backbone of Osiris.
description: The columnar sign shaped like a stylized tree trunk or spinal column, symbol of stability and of Osiris, whose backbone it was said to be. Set up as a temple emblem and raised by the king in the sed festival to renew his reign, it was also worn as an amulet; in the myth Isis and Nephthys restore the god beside it. Countless faience djed amulets survive from graves.

name: The Knot of Isis
powers: Guards the wearer through the power of Isis.
description: The looped red tjet amulet, the 'girdle of Isis,' worn by the living and the dead for the goddess's protection. Spell 156 of the Book of the Dead directs that it be made of red jasper and placed on the neck of the deceased so that Isis's might guards the throat. Red carnelian and faience tjets are common in New Kingdom burials, where they sit with the djed and ankh in protective groupings.
source: Book of the Dead, spell 156; amulet deposits

name: The Uraeus
powers: Spits fire against the king's enemies; guards the brow as the eye of Ra.
description: The rearing cobra worn on the brow of the pharaoh and of deities such as Ra, embodying the goddess Wadjet, protector of Lower Egypt. The uraeus spat fire at the king's foes and stood for the blazing eye that defended the sun god, and it was worn by kings and gods alike. Golden examples survive on royal diadems, most famously the cobra and vulture of Tutankhamun's gold mask.

name: The Senet Board
powers: Its play mirrored the soul's passage through the hazards of the afterlife.
description: The Egyptian board game of thirty squares in three rows, played with counters and knucklebones, the most common game board found in Egypt. The crossing of its hazardous squares mirrored the soul's journey through the afterlife, and the Book of the Dead shows the deceased playing senet against an invisible opponent to win passage. Complete boards, including Tutankhamun's, survive from royal tombs.
source: Excavated boards; Book of the Dead vignettes

name: The Palette of Narmer
powers: Ceremonial record of the king's victory and of the unification of the Two Lands.
description: A ceremonial siltstone palette from Hierakonpolis carved around 3100 BCE, showing King Narmer smiting an enemy and reviewing decapitated captives, long read as an early record of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. The falcon-god Horus perched above a bound foe and the king wielding a mace set the visual language of pharaonic royal power for three thousand years.

name: The War Shield of Neith
powers: Emblem of the goddess of war and of weaving.
description: The emblem of the goddess Neith of Sais: a shield across which two crossed arrows are set, combining her natures as a war goddess and a weaver. The symbol is attested as her sign from early Egyptian writing, painted on her temple walls and on votive objects, and the classical authors Plutarch and Herodotus described it. It is one of the oldest goddess emblems of Egypt.
source: Neith emblem on early votives; Plutarch, De Iside

name: The Wesekh Collar
powers: Bestowed solar protection and divine favor on its wearer.
description: The broad beaded collar worn across the chest by pharaohs, queens, and gods, built of rows of faience and semiprecious beads capped by golden falcon-headed terminals. Such collars were given as royal gifts and buried with the dead, who are shown receiving them from deities; Tutankhamun's burial yielded dozens in gold, glass, and stone. The wesekh lent its wearer solar protection and divine favor.

name: The Cup of Jamshid
powers: Reveals the whole world to the one who looks into it.
description: The cup of the legendary shah Jamshid, in which, according to the Shahnameh and later Persian tradition, the whole world could be seen as in a mirror, so that nothing was hidden from the king. The cup became a byword for far-seeing royal wisdom, and Persian poets used it as an image of mystical vision and self-knowledge. Its ties to the older idea of the king's divine glory are debated.

name: Rostam's Spear
powers: The heavy lance carried beside the mace and lasso in the hero's trials.
description: The heavy war-spear of the hero Rostam in the Shahnameh, carried alongside his bull-headed mace and lasso through the Haft Khan and the wars against Turan, and used to strike down champions in single combat. In Ferdowsi's epic it is one of the enormous plain weapons that suit his strength, wielded in duels such as the fateful fight with Sohrab. Its details follow epic convention.

name: The Feather of the Simurgh
powers: Burned as a signal, its smoke summons the great bird to help.
description: The feather given by the great bird Simurgh to the hero Zal and later to his son Rostam, to be burned whenever they needed the bird's aid, at whose smoke Simurgh came flying. In the Shahnameh the feather carries the abandoned boy Zal to safety and later rescues Rostam in his direst need. In later Sufi poetry it became an emblem of the soul's reliance on divine help.

name: The Mace of Faridun
maker: Forged for the young prince Faridun
powers: Struck down the tyrant Zahhak and freed Iran from his reign.
description: The bull-headed mace (gurz) forged for the young prince Faridun, which Ferdowsi describes being made to his measure before his campaign against the tyrant Zahhak. With it Faridun struck Zahhak's crowned head and split the serpents on his shoulders, ending a thousand years of tyranny and binding the usurper in a mountain cave. It became the archetypal weapon of Persian hero-kings.

name: The Derafsh Kaviani
material: Leather apron, gold, silk, jewels (later ornament)
maker: Kaveh the blacksmith; ornamented under Faridun
powers: Royal standard of Iran, carried before the shahs as a sign of popular revolt and kingship.
description: The leather apron of the blacksmith Kaveh, raised on a spear when he led the people of Iran against the tyrant Zahhak; the new king Faridun then adorned it with gold, silk, and jewels, and it became the royal standard of the Shahs under the name Derafsh Kaviani. The banner is retold each Newroz with Kaveh as a symbol of popular revolt and rightful rule.

name: The Belt of Tahmineh
powers: Binds the bond between the lady of Samangan and the hero Rostam.
description: A belt said to be woven by Tahmineh of Samangan, mother of Sohrab, and given to the hero Rostam on the night of their meeting, binding their union in some tellings of the tale. The motif varies across recensions of the Shahnameh and in modern retellings, and Ferdowsi's text describes no single canonical belt, so the object's particulars rest on later tradition rather than the epic's own lines.

name: The Arrow of Arash
powers: Its single flight fixed the boundary between Iran and Turan.
description: The arrow shot by Arash the archer from the summit of Mount Damavand to fix the frontier between Iran and Turan, a flight blessed in the myth by the giving of his own strength, covering hundreds of miles before falling on the far bank of the Oxus. Ferdowsi and earlier Persian sources recount how Arash was chosen for the feat, and modern poetry revived the story as a symbol of national sacrifice.

name: The Ruby of Qabus
aliases: Ruby of the Tower of Qabus
powers: A treasure gem of the Ziyarid ruler's court.
description: A great ruby linked in Persian legend and anecdote with Qabus, the Ziyarid ruler and patron of scholars remembered for the tower tomb of Gonbad-e Qabus. The gem is said to have been kept among his treasures or set in his regalia, but no named early source describes it in any detail, and the surviving references belong to later literary tradition. Its particulars therefore cannot be verified.

name: The Seal of Solomon
material: Gold ring set with a stone (mythic)
powers: By its engraving of the divine Name, its bearer commanded the winds, beasts, and jinn.
description: The signet ring of the prophet-king Solomon, engraved with the divine Name, by whose power he commanded the winds, beasts, and jinn in Jewish and Islamic tradition alike, told in the Quran, the midrash, and the Thousand and One Nights. Its seal, often drawn as a six-pointed star, later became a widespread protective emblem across the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe.
source: Quran; midrash; Thousand and One Nights

name: Solomon's Flying Carpet
powers: Carried the king, his throne, and his court through the air on the wind.
description: The carpet of Solomon, woven of silk and green stuff, said in Islamic tradition to be large enough to bear the king, his throne, and his whole court, carried through the air by the wind at his command and shaded by a flock of birds overhead. The Quran records the wind as made subject to Solomon, and later commentators expanded this into the famous flying carpet, whose details grow in the tellings.
source: Quran; al-Tabari; al-Kisa'i; Thousand and One Nights

name: Aladdin's Lamp
powers: Rubbed, it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes.
description: The lamp of the tale of Aladdin, added to the Thousand and One Nights by Antoine Galland from the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab around 1709. Rubbing it summoned a powerful jinni who granted wishes, while its twin, the magician's lamp, drove the plot's theft and recovery. No medieval Arabic original of the tale survives, so the lamp is a literary invention of the folk tradition.

name: The Magic Carpet of the Nights
powers: Bore its riders through the air to distant lands.
description: The flying carpet of the Thousand and One Nights cycle and of later oriental folklore, a woven rug that carried its riders through the air to far-off countries. Within the Nights corpus itself the carpet appears chiefly in the tale of Prince Husayn in the later 'Forty Wazirs' addition, and much of its modern fame comes from European retellings. Its details vary widely from one telling to another.

name: The Bottle of the Ifrit
powers: Held a vast ifrit imprisoned for centuries until a fisherman freed him.
description: The sealed copper bottle cast up in the fisherman's net in the Thousand and One Nights tale of the Fisherman and the Jinni, from which a vast ifrit escaped in a pillar of smoke and threatened to kill his liberator. The fisherman tricked the spirit back into the vessel by doubting that so great a being could fit. The jar is the archetype of the bottled-jinn motif in world folklore.
source: Thousand and One Nights, The Fisherman and the Jinni

name: Sefer Yetzirah
maker: Tradition attributes it to the patriarch Abraham
powers: Describes the creation of the world through the Hebrew letters and the ten sefirot.
description: The earliest surviving Hebrew text of Jewish mysticism, the 'Book of Formation,' which describes how the world was created through the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet and the ten sefirot, and sets out paths by which the mystic may emulate that act. Its opening lines attribute it to the patriarch Abraham, and it shaped the whole later development of Kabbalah.

name: The Temple Menorah
powers: The seven-branched lampstand kept alight in the sanctuary.
description: The seven-branched golden lampstand of the Tabernacle and later of the Jerusalem Temple, prescribed in the Book of Exodus as a beaten-gold work with almond-shaped cups and blossoms, kept burning in the sanctuary. Its image survives on the Arch of Titus relief and throughout Jewish art, and its fate after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE became a theme of Jewish legend and diaspora memory.
source: Book of Exodus; Arch of Titus relief

name: The Ark of the Covenant
powers: Carried before Israel and kept in the Holy of Holies as the throne of God's presence.
description: The gilded chest built at Sinai to hold the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, carried before the Israelites and kept in the Holy of Holies of the Jerusalem Temple. Legend holds it was hidden before the Babylonian destruction, while Ethiopian tradition claims it rests at Aksum. Its descriptions come from the biblical books; no archaeological witness survives.

name: The Brazen Serpent
powers: Healed the Israelites bitten by desert serpents when they looked upon it.
description: The bronze serpent made by Moses at God's command to heal the Israelites bitten by serpents in the wilderness, raised on a pole so that the stricken who looked upon it lived. Kept in the Jerusalem Temple, it was later destroyed by King Hezekiah as an idol under the name Nehushtan. Its story is told in Numbers and 2 Kings, and the object itself is known only from scripture.

name: The Sword of Goliath
powers: The heavy blade of the Philistine champion, kept as a relic at Nob.
description: The sword of the Philistine champion Goliath, taken as spoil after David slew him and later kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at the sanctuary of Nob, where the fugitive David received it, saying there was none like it. The weapon is described in the First Book of Samuel, and David's possession of it anchors his kingship narrative in the biblical account.

name: The Grail of Qumran
aliases: Holy Grail of the Dead Sea
powers: None attested; a modern identification without support.
description: A drinking vessel that popular speculation has linked with the Dead Sea Scrolls community at Qumran and identified with the Holy Grail of Christian legend. No manuscript, inscription, or excavation connects any Qumran cup to the Grail tradition, and the identification is a modern theory built on suggestion rather than any primary source. It is a derived claim, not an attested artifact.

name: The Khamsa
powers: Deflects the evil eye and brings blessing to its bearer.
description: The open-hand amulet of the Maghreb and wider Middle East, called the Hand of Fatima after the Prophet's daughter and the Hand of Miriam in Jewish usage, hung in homes, worn as jewelry, and painted on doorways against the evil eye. The silver khamsa was the standard talisman of North African Jews and Muslims alike, with pieces from sheet silver to fine filigree set with coral.

name: The Gris-gris
maker: Fqih (learned man) who wrote the contents
powers: Protects, heals, or brings luck by the written words sealed inside.
description: A small leather pouch worn on the body, holding written Qur'anic verses, prayers, or magic squares, used across North Africa to protect, heal, or bring fortune. In Morocco the hirz was stitched by a fqih and worn at the neck or arm, its power resting entirely on the writing sealed inside. The custom is documented in ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice and survives today.
source: Ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice

name: The Tunisian Fibula
powers: Fastened the shawl and served as a bridal heirloom and protective talisman.
description: The large silver pin or brooch, often triangular with a central coral or enamel stud and a long pointed pin, worn by Amazigh women across Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco to fasten the shawl and passed down as a bridal heirloom. Its form echoes Roman-era brooches of the region, and its silver and coral decoration is documented in museum collections of Maghrebi dress.

name: The Sword of Antar
powers: The great blade of the warrior-poet, wielded in his duels and tribal wars.
description: The sword Dhami, the chosen blade of Antarah ibn Shaddad, the pre-Islamic warrior-poet of the Arabian Peninsula whose exploits fill the medieval romance Sirah 'Antar. In the sira, Antar wins the sword in combat and carries it through the wars of the tribe of Abs and his long struggle to marry Abla. The romance is literary, and the sword's named exploits grow with the telling.

name: The Jambiya
powers: Symbol of honor and manhood; drawn in the bara' dance.
description: The short curved dagger with a broad double-edged blade worn at the belt by Yemeni men, a symbol of honor and manhood carried from youth and drawn in the bara' war dance. Silver-sheathed jambiya hilts, some of rhino horn, are treasured heirlooms and marks of tribal standing. The weapon is attested across Yemeni material culture and in the dances, songs, and poetry that surround it.
source: Yemeni material culture and ethnographic records

name: Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi
powers: Said to command the wind and fell whole fields of grass; one of the Three Sacred Treasures.
description: The legendary grass-cutting sword drawn from the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi by Susanoo, then offered to Amaterasu and placed among the Three Sacred Treasures of the Japanese imperial regalia. Kept today at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, it is said to command the wind and cut down an entire field of grass in a single stroke.

name: Yata no Kagami
powers: Reflects truth and brilliance; part of the imperial regalia.
description: The Eight-Fold Mirror hung from a sacred sakaki tree outside the cave where Amaterasu hid, its brilliance luring the sun goddess back to illuminate the world. Revered at Ise Grand Shrine as one of the Three Sacred Treasures, it stands for truth and for the imperial line's legitimacy in Japanese myth.

name: Yasakani no Magatama
powers: Symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's right to rule.
description: The curved jade bead (magatama) dangled from the branch of the sacred sakaki tree beside the mirror that drew Amaterasu from her cave. Counted among the Three Sacred Treasures of Japan, it symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's mandate, and its comma shape recurs in tomb jewelry from the Kofun period.

name: Shichishito
powers: None (honorific and ritual sword)
description: An iron sword with seven branch-like projections along the blade, dedicated to the Isonokami Shrine and recorded in the Nihon Shoki as a gift from the kingdom of Baekje. Its long inlaid inscription describing offerings to the sun deity makes it a rare physical relic of early Korean-Japanese exchange and a treasure of Japanese shrine keeping.

name: Hannya Mask
powers: Embodies a woman turned demon by jealousy
description: A Noh theatre mask sculpted as the face of a woman twisted by jealousy into a horned, serpent-eyed demon, with metal fangs and a grimacing mouth. Carried by performers in plays such as Dojoji and Aoi no Ue, the hannya shows obsession consuming the living into demonic form, and the mask itself is held to retain dangerous power.

name: Oni no Kanabo
powers: Said to crush any demon or mortal it strikes
description: The iron-studded club that Japanese tales and art place in the grip of the oni, the red-and-blue ogre of legend. Treated as a stock attribute of the ogre rather than a documented artifact, it appears in tales from Shuten-doji onward, its weight said to crush whatever it strikes; no historical example survives.

name: Shimenawa
powers: Marks off divine ground and repels impurity
description: A sacred rope twisted from rice straw and hung before shrines, torii gates, and sacred trees to mark off divine ground. Its origin is tied to the rope strung across the cave mouth after Amaterasu emerged, preventing the sun goddess from retreating; the shimenawa now seals off the kami's dwelling places from impurity.

name: Hagoromo
powers: Lets its wearer fly between heaven and earth
description: The feather mantle that lets a heavenly maiden (tennyo) fly between the mortal world and the sky. In the classic Noh play Hagoromo, a fisherman of Mio Bay finds one hung on a pine and makes the angel dance before returning it; the robe marks the tenuous boundary between human and divine realms in Japanese drama and folklore.
source: Noh play Hagoromo; coastal legend tradition

name: Kitsune's Crescent Comb
powers: Reveals a fox in human form; granting it service or love
description: The crescent-shaped comb that Japanese tales say a shapeshifting kitsune drops when its fox tail is betrayed. A man who finds one may gain the fox's love or service, and the comb recurs as the tell-tale clue in tales of fox wives whose disguise slips at midnight, linking the small hair ornament to the oldest fox legends of Japan.

name: Daruma Doll
powers: Talisman of perseverance and wish fulfillment
description: A rounded paper-mache doll modeled on Bodhidharma, the first Zen patriarch, whose hollow weighted body always rocks back upright. Bought as a talisman of perseverance, its eyes are inked one at a time as a wish is granted, and the year's dolls are burned in temple ceremonies that close out the warding of ill fortune.

name: Ruyi Jingu Bang
powers: Shrinks and grows at the wearer's will; weighs thirteen thousand five hundred catties
description: The magic staff of Sun Wukong the Monkey King, pulled from the East Sea Dragon Palace where it stood as a pillar weighing thirteen thousand five hundred catties. It shrank and grew at its bearer's will, and its gold-banded ends helped the Monkey King defy the heavenly host before he was pressed into escorting the pilgrim Tripitaka to the West.

name: Jiu Ding
powers: Signifies the Mandate of Heaven and legitimacy of rule
description: The nine bronze tripods (jiu ding) that culture hero Yu the Great is said to have cast from tribute metal gathered across the Nine Provinces, inscribing each region's creatures so the people could recognize them. Passed between the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties as the physical warrant of the Mandate of Heaven, they became the archetype of legitimate rule in Chinese historiography.

name: Hou Yi's Bow
powers: Shot down nine of the ten suns
description: The red bow of the legendary archer Hou Yi, who in Chinese myth shot down nine of the ten suns that scorched the earth, leaving one to light the day. His skill earned him the elixir of immortality, and his bow remains the emblem of marksmanship in tales of the heavenly archer and his doomed wife Chang'e.

name: Elixir of Immortality
powers: Bestows eternal life
description: The drug of immortality that Hou Yi obtained from the Queen Mother of the West. His wife Chang'e swallowed it to keep it from a thief and drifted to the moon, where she lives forever in the cold lunar palace with the jade rabbit; the tale, recorded in Han-era sources, gave the moon its goddess and the Mid-Autumn Festival its story.

name: Jade Rabbit's Mortar
powers: Pounds the elixir of immortality
description: The mortar and pestle with which the Jade Rabbit pounds the elixir of immortality on the moon, a familiar figure in Mid-Autumn Festival imagery. The rabbit is said to grind herbs under the cassia tree for Chang'e, and the same moon-rabbit motif recurs across East Asian lore, including Korean tales of a rabbit on the lunar surface.
source: Han bronze mirrors and moon-rabbit tradition

name: Bagua Mirror
powers: Deflects harmful energy (sha qi) and returns evil glances
description: A circular mirror ringed with the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes around a central yin-yang disc, hung over doorways in Chinese feng shui practice to turn away harmful energy (sha qi). Also paired with talismanic spells against hauntings, the bagua mirror is said to return an attacker's evil gaze and to guard the threshold from malign spirits.

name: Guan Dao
material: Steel blade on a long wooden shaft
powers: Emblem of martial protection and the god of war
description: The heavy curved-blade polearm historically carried by Guan Yu, the Three Kingdoms general deified as the god of war. The 'Green Dragon Crescent Blade' is the most famous of its kind; ceremonial guan dao are still kept in martial temples and used in lion-dance and martial-arts displays to invoke his protection.

name: Flaming Pearl
powers: Signifies wisdom, wealth, and transformation
description: A luminous pearl wreathed in flame (huozhu) depicted in Chinese art as the treasure two dragons chase or guard. Linked to the dragon's undersea realm and to Buddhist wish-granting jewels, the flaming pearl symbolizes wisdom, wealth, and transformation, and it appears on temple roofs, ceramics, and paintings across East Asia.
source: Dragon art motif; Buddhist jewel tradition

name: The Heavenly Loom
powers: Wove the patterned clouds of the sky
description: The celestial loom of Zhinü, the Weaver Girl, who wove the patterned clouds of the sky beside the Heavenly River. When her marriage to the cowherd Niulang made her neglect her weaving, the Jade Emperor separated the pair, and on the seventh night of the seventh month magpies bridge the river for their yearly reunion, the origin of the Qixi festival.
source: Qixi legend; Han to Tang sources

name: Cheonbuin
powers: Marks the royal mandate of the founder king
description: The heavenly seal that the Samguk Yusa says Hwanung, son of the sky god Hwanin, carried when he descended to Mount Taebaek with three seals to govern the world. Given to his descendants as the mark of royal mandate, the seal anchors the Dangun foundation myth in which the bear-woman Ungnyeo's son Dangun founded the first Korean kingdom.

name: Geobukseon
powers: Iron-roofed warship that shed fire and boarding parties
description: The armored turtle warship built for Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet in the 1590s, roofed with an iron-studded shell that shed flame and repelled boarders. Though a real historical vessel, it passed into Korean folklore as an invincible protector of the coast, celebrated in songs and tales of the Imjin War against the Japanese invasion.

name: Gogok
powers: Symbol of rank, fertility, and the sun
description: The comma-shaped jade ornament threaded onto the gold crowns and belts of the Silla kingdom and excavated in numbers from the tombs of Gyeongju. Scholars link the curved bead to the bear-woman Ungnyeo's offering in the Dangun myth and to shamanic fertility symbolism; it remains the emblem of ancient Korean royal regalia.

name: Bangmangi
powers: Grants whatever the wielder wishes when struck
description: The magic club (bangmangi) of the Korean goblin dokkaebi, which in folktales grants whatever a person wishes when it strikes. Villagers trick the gullible dokkaebi into beating the club and losing it, or use it to draw endless food, gold, and healing; the club and its owner remain beloved fixtures of Korean storytelling.

name: Thuan Thien Sword
powers: Granted victory over the Ming invaders
description: The magic sword Thuan Thien ('Heaven's Will') given to the farmer-emperor Le Loi by the golden turtle god Kim Qui during his revolt against Ming rule. After his victory the turtle surfaced on Hoan Kiem Lake to reclaim the blade, giving the lake its name, the Lake of the Returned Sword.

name: Betel and Areca Tray
powers: Foundation of hospitality and marriage ritual
description: The tray that carries betel leaves, areca nut, and lime, the foundation of Vietnamese hospitality and marriage custom. In the founding legend, twin brothers Cao and Lang died for love of the same woman and became the areca tree and betel vine; chewing the combination remains a rite of respect, greeting, and kinship.
source: Betel and areca legend; folk custom

name: The Jade Emperor's Gong
powers: Summoned rain when struck by the frog
description: In a Vietnamese folk tale, a frog led a deputation of animals to heaven to complain that rain never fell, then beat the Jade Emperor's own bronze gong until the god sent rain. The gong is a story element rather than a documented artifact, and the tale survives chiefly through oral retellings across the Red River delta.

name: Co Loa Crossbow
powers: Each shot could slay thousands
description: The magic crossbow of An Duong Vuong, its trigger made from the golden turtle-claw that Kim Qui gave the king at Co Loa. Each shot could kill thousands, but when the king's daughter My Chau revealed the secret to her husband Trong Thuy, the stolen trigger lost the citadel to the enemy.

name: The Emerald Buddha's Robes
aliases: Royal Vestments of the Emerald Buddha
powers: Palladium of the Thai kingdom
description: The three robes of gold worn by the Emerald Buddha in the Wat Phra Kaew temple in Bangkok and changed at the turn of each season in a ceremony performed by the king. The jeweled garments, their alternation fixed by royal ritual, mark the image as the palladium of the Thai state and the axis of the kingdom's legitimacy.

name: The Naga's Jewel
powers: Grants wealth and kingship to its holder
description: The luminous gem that the naga, the great serpent of the Mekong, is said to guard in the watery underworld, granting wealth and kingship to whoever obtains it. Retold in Thai and Lao river lore, the jewel is also linked to the fireballs that rise from the river during the full moon festival of the eleventh lunar month.

name: The Bayon Smile
powers: The king's watchful presence over the kingdom
description: The colossal stone face-towers of the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom, carved in the 12th century under Jayavarman VII with serene, downcast smiles. Khmer legend reads the many faces as the king's presence watching over the kingdom from every direction, and the towers remain the emblem of Angkor's guardian gaze.

name: The Four White Umbrellas
powers: Emblems of the right to rule granted from above
description: The white-tiered umbrellas that the Burmese chronicles place among the regalia of the first kings, emblems of the right to rule granted from above. Their role in the creation tale of kingship binds earthly sovereignty to the nats, and umbrella standards still crown Burmese pagodas and throne halls as marks of sacred authority.

name: The Relic of That Phanom
powers: Focus of veneration; guardian presence of the Mekong
description: The relic of the Buddha's breastbone enshrined at That Phanom on the Mekong, the most revered stupa of Laos and northeastern Thailand. Lao legend holds that a naga king, Phanya Sithan, invited the monks and guarded the shrine site, binding the sacred chedi to the river's serpentine protectors.

name: Khaen
powers: Voice of lam song and festival celebration
description: The free-reed mouth organ of Laos built from rows of bamboo tubes bound around a wooden wind-chest, its drone-and-melody sound the soul of lam folk song. Played at festivals, rituals, and courtship, the khaen is credited by Lao tradition with shaping the speech and poetry of the people.

name: The Golden Whip of Genghis Khan
powers: Said to rally and reward warriors of the khan
description: The golden whip that legend says Genghis Khan carried, brandished to rally and reward his warriors, and in some tellings the source of his military genius. No such whip survives or is named in the Secret History; the story is a modern heroic retelling of the conqueror's rise rather than a documented relic.

name: The Whistling Arrow
powers: Signal whistle that directed cavalry maneuvers
description: The signal arrow of the Mongol armies, tipped with a drilled bone head that shrieked in flight, used by Genghis Khan's cavalry to direct charges and ambushes across the steppe. Described by Persian and Chinese chroniclers, the whistling arrow survives as a motif of the swift, coordinated warfare that built the empire.
source: Persian and Chinese chronicles of the Mongol campaigns

name: Morin Khuur
powers: Voice of the horse and the steppe
description: The two-stringed horse-head fiddle of Mongolia, its scroll carved as a horse's head and its strings and bow made of horsehair. Legend tells of a herdsman whose beloved horse was killed, and who made the fiddle from its remains to keep the horse's song alive; it is now an emblem of Mongolian national identity.

name: Tsagaan Tug
powers: Ensign of khanly authority and national unity
description: The white standard (tsagaan tug) that Mongol tradition honors as the ensign of Genghis Khan's lineage, kept at the mausoleum complex in Ordos and paraded with the nine black banners at the Naadam festival. Its horsehair crown and spear shaft mark the enduring authority of the steppe khans.

name: Phurba
powers: Pins down demons during exorcism rituals
description: The three-sided ritual dagger of Tibetan Buddhism, its pommel carved with a wrathful deity's head and its blade meant to pin down demonic forces. Used by lamas in exorcism, the phurba transfixes evil at the axis between the worlds, and inscribed iron examples survive in temple collections.
source: Tibetan tantric ritual tradition; temple collections

name: Prayer Wheel
material: Metal and wood over a paper scroll
powers: Releases mantra prayers with each turn
description: The cylindrical wheel, rolled or spun in the hand, that Tibetan Buddhist practice turns to release the mantras printed inside, each revolution sending the prayer for compassion into the world. Rows of wheels line temple and stupa walls, and the device descends from Indian and Tibetan ritual turning of sacred verses.

name: Yeouiju
powers: Grants wishes; lets the imugi become a dragon
description: The wish-granting jewel (yeouiju) of Korean lore, the prize that a serpent imugi must grasp to climb into dragonhood. Said to grant any wish to its holder, it appears in tales of serpents waiting years for the jewel to fall from the sky, as in the story of the imugi that lost it at the waterfall.
